title: How Big Bang Theory Works, with Neil deGrasse Tyson
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Big Bang theory: what it does and does not describe, the expansion of space rather than an explosion, the history from spectroscopes, Doppler effect and Hubble's observations, Einstein's static-universe view, predictions like the cosmic microwave background, the early timeline from the Planck-era fractions of a second through baryogenesis, nucleosynthesis and recombination, the formation of structure from quantum fluctuations, dark matter and the fate of the universe, the flatness problem, criticisms, and alternative models (steady state, ekpyrotic, plasma cosmology). The episode closes with an interview with astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson about the observational basis of the theory, the limits of science before the Big Bang, string theory and quantum gravity, and how scientific progress happens. Ends with listener mail about whether Russia is a European country.

segments.title: Opening banter and Tyson interview setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on the Big Bang theory, mention they interviewed Neil deGrasse Tyson at the Fox Theater, and joke about his quotes. Chuck leaves the room and Josh continues.

segments.title: What the Big Bang theory is and is not
segments.summary: The Big Bang is a well-supported theory describing the early universe, not its origin. It is not an explosion in space but the rapid expansion of space itself from a hot, dense singularity. The hosts discuss the analogies used and the limits of science near the start of time.

segments.title: Early universe conditions and the four forces
segments.summary: The hosts describe the extreme density and heat of the early universe, the four fundamental forces being unified at the start, and the search for a theory of everything. They note that physics breaks down closer to the singularity.

segments.title: History: spectroscopes, Doppler effect and Hubble
segments.summary: The history of the theory: spectroscopes in the 1800s, Christian Doppler's work on sound and frequency shifts, and Edwin Hubble's finding that distant stars' velocities relate to their distance, suggesting expansion. Einstein initially believed in a static universe, then accepted expansion.

segments.title: Predictions: homogeneity, isotropy and cosmic microwave background
segments.summary: Predictions of the expansion theory include that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic with no center, and that leftover radiation from the early universe would be evenly distributed. This cosmic microwave background was detected and later supports the theory, along with gravitational wave evidence.

segments.title: Timeline of the first second: Planck time to standard cosmology
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the early timeline, from the earliest point science can reason about, through the separation of forces, baryogenesis with slightly more matter than antimatter, and the start of standard cosmology at about 0.01 seconds, when protons and neutrons formed.

segments.title: Atoms, transparency and cosmic microwave background
segments.summary: After about 380,000 years, the universe cooled enough for protons and electrons to form atoms and light could travel, making the universe transparent. The hosts give current temperature of space and discuss the cooling and expansion.

segments.title: Formation of stars, galaxies and the fate of the universe
segments.summary: Quantum fluctuations grew over time into regions of higher density that drew matter together, forming stars, galaxies and clusters. The hosts discuss the entropy objection, dark matter, whether the universe will keep expanding or collapse in a Big Crunch, and the flatness problem.

segments.title: Criticisms and alternative models of the universe
segments.summary: Criticisms include violation of the first law of thermodynamics and faster-than-light inflation, which proponents answer by saying the laws may not apply that early. Alternatives discussed are steady state, the ekpyrotic (colliding branes) model, and plasma cosmology.

segments.title: Neil deGrasse Tyson interview: evidence, multiverse and string theory
segments.summary: In the interview, Tyson says the expanding universe picture rests on data and was built over about ninety years starting with Hubble, discusses multiverse ideas, the gap between quantum physics and general relativity, and string theory as the main effort to unify them.

segments.title: Interview conclusion and listener mail: Is Russia European?
segments.summary: Tyson comments on how science advances through large collaborations such as LIGO and the Higgs boson search, and on his early interest in science. The hosts then read listener mail arguing that Russia is historically a European country, with most of its population in the European part.
